Step 1

The body is full of hydrogen

The body is mostly water, carbohydrates and proteins. All three are rich in hydrogen atoms. The nucleus of each hydrogen atom behaves like a tiny spinning magnet. That property is called spin, and it is what an MRI machine works with.

SpinThe property that makes each hydrogen nucleus act like a tiny spinning magnet.

Why hydrogen? It is the one ingredient the three main building blocks share, so there is plenty of it to measure everywhere in the body.

Step 2

A superconducting magnet lines them up

The machine uses a large superconducting magnet, chilled with liquid helium. Enormous currents flow through it with zero resistance. Those circulating currents create a very strong magnetic field.

Superconducting magnetCooled with liquid helium so huge currents flow with zero resistance. It makes the main field, B₀.

The field forces all the hydrogen protons to align neatly along the machine’s longitudinal axis, the long axis running through the tube.

Longitudinal axisThe long axis of the tube, drawn as z. Protons line up along it in the main field.
Step 3

A burst of radio waves tips them over

A second set of coils, the RF (radiofrequency) coils, delivers a burst of radio waves. The energy knocks the tiny magnets sideways. They then wobble together, in sync, in the transverse plane (the plane across the body, at right angles to the main field).

RF coilsSend the burst of radio waves that tips the protons sideways.
Transverse planeThe plane across the tube, at right angles to the main field, where the tipped protons wobble together.
Step 4

Detector coils pick up the wobble

At this moment, detector coils placed near the body pick up the collective wobble as an oscillating signal.

Detector coilsSit near the body and pick up the combined wobble as an oscillating signal.

The problem. On its own this signal is just one big noise. It says something is wobbling but not where. Step 5 fixes that.

Step 5

Gradient coils give the signal a location

Large spiral coils, the gradient coils, are switched on. They create tiny variations in the magnetic field, so protons in different parts of the body wobble at slightly different phases.

Gradient coilsLarge spiral coils that vary the field slightly across the body, so protons wobble at different phases.

That turns the signal into striped patterns: black and white bands that encode spatial information.

Step 6

Relaxation tells the tissues apart

When the RF and gradient coils switch off, the spins gradually lose sync and drift back to their original alignment along the main field. This return is called relaxation.

RelaxationSpins losing sync and returning to alignment, at a different speed in each tissue.

This recovery happens at different speeds in different tissues. That difference is what makes fat, muscle and fluids distinguishable in the final image.

Step 7

Repeat it to build a library of patterns

Each activation of the system captures one striped pattern. The machine repeats the process many times with different gradient settings and timings, and collects a whole library of patterns.

From one capture to the next, the stripes change direction and get finer. Each one holds a different piece of the picture.

Step 8

A Fourier transform makes the picture

All the patterns are combined mathematically using a Fourier transform. This converts them into a sharp, high-contrast image.

Fourier transformThe mathematical step that combines all the striped patterns into one image.

The machine does this slice by slice, and the stack of slices builds a complete 3D scan of the body.

More patterns, sharper image. As more patterns are combined, the blurry image becomes clear.

Going deeper

How the Fourier transform works

A Fourier transform takes a signal and tells you which frequencies it is made of, and how much of each. It works because any signal can be built by adding sine waves of different frequencies. A piano chord is one messy sound wave, yet you hear separate notes in it. The transform splits a signal back into its notes.

FrequencyHow many times a wave repeats in a given time or distance.

To test for one frequency, multiply the signal by a pure sine wave of that frequency, point by point, and average the result. If the signal contains that frequency, the product is mostly positive and the average is large. If it does not, the positive and negative parts cancel and the average is about zero. Repeat the test for every frequency and you get the chart at the bottom of Fig. 10.

In MRI the same idea works in two ways. With a gradient on, protons at different positions wobble at different frequencies, so each frequency in the signal carries the signal from one position. In two dimensions, an image can be built from stripe patterns of different directions and widths. Each captured pattern measures how much of one stripe pattern is in the image. Adding them all back together gives the picture.

Inverse Fourier transformAdds the stripe patterns back together to rebuild the image. The forward transform goes the other way, from a signal to its frequencies.

Why the centre is brightest. The broad stripes are the strongest part of most images, so k-space is brightest at its centre. The fine stripes add the sharpness, which is why more patterns give a sharper image.
